## The idea

The white notes from C to the next C have a familiar shape, even before you can
name it. Begin the same white-note walk on D, however, and the balance changes.
The keys still look alike under your fingers; what changed is the sequence of
gaps between them. That sequence is the useful object. A *major scale* follows
the ordered step formula `2, 2, 1, 2, 2, 2, 1`, with every number measured in
semitones.

Learning scales as rows of note names makes each key feel like a new item to
memorise. The formula gives a better account: one construction can
begin on any root. It also directs the ear to the scale's two tight places. The
one-semitone steps fall between degrees 3 and 4, then between 7 and 8. Shift one
of those small gaps and you have not made a faulty major scale. You have made a
different interval pattern with a different sound.

## Run this

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 112
use_synth :pluck

define :build_scale do |root, steps|
  notes = [root]
  steps.each { |step| notes << notes[-1] + step }
  notes
end

define :play_phrase do |notes|
  notes.each do |pitch|
    play pitch, release: 0.32
    sleep 0.5
  end
end

major_steps = [2, 2, 1, 2, 2, 2, 1]
c_major = build_scale(note(:c4), major_steps)

play_phrase c_major
play_phrase c_major.reverse

thirds = [0, 2, 1, 3, 2, 4, 3, 5, 4, 6, 5, 7]
play_phrase thirds.map { |index| c_major[index] }

(60...72).each do |root|
  ours = build_scale(root, major_steps)
  sonic_pi = scale(root, :major).to_a
  puts "root #{root}: #{ours == sonic_pi}"
end
```

The first pass makes the formula plain by climbing and descending one degree at
a time. The later pass skips alternate degrees. Nothing has been added to the
pitch collection, yet the skips begin to suggest harmony and give the line more
direction. Meanwhile, the log checks a separate question: for each possible
root, does our constructor return the same pitches as Sonic Pi's major scale?
Each `true` confirms that agreement.

## Change one thing

1. Change the root from `:c4` to `:fs3`. Follow the two one-semitone gaps as the
   whole pattern moves into a lower register. Their positions within the scale
   do not change, even though every sounding pitch does.
2. Change the fourth value in `major_steps` from `2` to `1`. The last note now
   falls a semitone short of the octave. Because the function accumulates
   distances, the missing semitone affects every later destination.
3. Play `c_major.values_at(0, 2, 4, 7)` slowly. The first three selected pitches
   outline a chord; the last supplies the upper tonic. Remove index `7` and
   listen to the difference between an implied harmony and a completed octave.

## Why it works

Each number in `major_steps` is a delta rather than a pitch. `build_scale`
starts with the root, adds one delta, saves the result, and repeats. In
programming terms it is a cumulative sum that preserves its intermediate
states, like a running balance or a route reconstructed from segment lengths.
That model explains why editing one early step moves everything that follows.

The seven steps add to twelve, so the eighth note arrives exactly one octave
above the root. Five steps are whole tones of two semitones; two are semitones.
Their order, rather than their mere presence, gives major its shape. Rotating
the same values moves the tight gaps and produces the modes in Lesson 24.
Changing only the root is transposition, since every result receives the same
offset and every internal interval survives.

The comparison loop turns that claim into a small test. One C-major example
could succeed by accident, so the loop checks all twelve pitch classes against
Sonic Pi's built-in constructor. Ruby can establish that the returned arrays
match element by element. It cannot establish how clearly a synth exposes the
two semitone steps, which is why the run combines inspection with listening.

## Take it further

Write `descending_scale(root, steps)` without calling `reverse`. Begin at
`root + 12` and subtract the step values in reverse order until the line reaches
`root`. Print both directions for all twelve roots before playing the pair in F
major. Each array should contain eight notes, and the top note of the ascent
should be the starting note of the descent. Those checks tell you whether the
arithmetic closes before the sound has a chance to disguise an off-by-one error.
